reason: The chapter's top-ranked candidate at this verse and it is an accident of English word order. Ether 6:2 has 'the brother of Jared came down out of the mount, and he did put forth the stones'; Judges 3:27 has 'he blew a trumpet in the mountain of Ephraim, and the children of Israel went down with him from the mount, and he before them'. The shared run straddles a clause boundary in both and consists of an article, a noun the Book of Mormon has already used four times in Ether 3 for Shelem, and a pronoun. Ehud's muster after the killing of Eglon has no contact of any kind with the lighting of the barges. Covered here rather than passed over in silence only because it is the sole candidate the machine offered for a verse that does have a genuine source, adjudicated at 6:3.

Ether 6:4 ends 'commending themselves unto the Lord their God'; Numbers 6:2 has men and women who 'separate themselves unto the LORD' by the vow of a Nazarite. The four words are a reflexive pronoun and a prepositional phrase, and the verbs they attach to are unrelated — commending is entrusting, separating is consecrating. Nothing else of the Nazarite legislation is anywhere near this chapter. The Jeremiah 3:7, Amos 7:2 and Joshua 5:8 candidates at this same verse are 'and it came to pass' and 'had done all these things' and are covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

sharedText: upon the waves of the sea
reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and the one most likely to tempt a reader, because it shares six consecutive words with Ether 6:5 and because both sentences are about God and the sea. It is declined on distribution and on sense. “waves of the sea” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Job 9:8, Psalm 93:4, Isaiah 48:18 and Jude 1:13 — which is not rare enough to identify a source for a phrase this ordinary, and the preposition that completes the run is doing opposite work in the two texts: Job's God treads upon the waves, walking on them in sovereignty, while Ether's Jaredites are tossed upon them, helpless. Job 9:8 is a hymn to divine transcendence in a speech about the impossibility of contending with God; Ether 6:5 is a report of a voyage. The verse's real source is adjudicated at 6:5 (Genesis 8:1, with Genesis 7:18), and the storm sequence it belongs to at 6:7 (Psalm 107).

A four-word run and a real one: 'And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam'. But 'the LORD God caused' is the KJV's ordinary way of narrating any divine act with a causative verb, and the object here is a surgical anaesthetic in Eden. The temptation is worth naming because the chapter genuinely is running Genesis — but it is running Genesis 7-11, not Genesis 2, and the borrowing at this verse is 'the face of the waters' and 'a wind', both of which come from the flood. Filed as wrong-sense rather than formulaic because a reader who noticed that Ether 6 is a creation-and-flood chapter might reasonably take the Eden verse for evidence of it.

'Because of the mountain waves which broke upon them' against 'Because of the mountain of Zion, which is desolate, the foxes walk upon it'. The match ends exactly where the content begins: Lamentations' next word is 'of', introducing a genitive, and Ether's next word is 'waves', making 'mountain' an attributive adjective — a use the KJV never makes of the word. 'Mountain waves' is not a biblical construction at all, which is the interesting fact here and the reason the entry is written: the most vivid image in the Jaredite storm is one of the few phrases in the chapter with no King James background.

“the fierceness of” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and in nine of them the genitive is anger, wrath or indignation; the tenth, Jeremiah 25:38, has 'the fierceness of the oppressor'. Ether 6:6 has 'the fierceness of the wind'. The Book of Mormon has taken a KJV idiom for the intensity of rage and applied it to weather, which is a small stylistic observation and not a dependence on any one verse. Jeremiah 25:38's lion forsaking his covert has nothing to do with a storm at sea.

Typology pulls hard here. Isaiah 43:2 — 'When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned' — is the Bible's standing promise that water will not hurt the covenant people, and Ether 6:7 says 'there was no water that could hurt them'. But there is not one distinctive shared word. Isaiah's verbs are pass, overflow, walk, burn; Ether's are hurt, encompass, cry, bring forth. “no water” occurs in exactly seventeen KJV verses and every one of them is about drought or an empty pit, which is the opposite problem. Recorded so that a reader who sees the Isaiah promise behind the barges is told the catalogue saw it too and declined it; the deliverance language at this verse comes from Psalm 107:28, adjudicated at 6:7.

sharedText: the Lord all the day long
reason: A six-word run, and the second-highest score in the chapter, and worthless. “the day long” occurs in exactly thirteen KJV verses, spread across Deuteronomy, the Psalms and Proverbs, and it attaches indifferently to boasting, mourning, being plagued, coveting and being killed. Proverbs 23:17's own sentence is 'be thou in the fear of the LORD all the day long', a warning against envying sinners; Ether 6:9 is a doxology on a boat. The run scores because 'the LORD' happens to precede the adverbial in Proverbs, which is a fact about the two English word orders. The verse's real contact is Psalm 68:32, adjudicated at 6:9.

'And the brother of Jared also begat sons and daughters' reproduces, word for word, a clause that stands in exactly eighteen KJV verses, all but one of them in the antediluvian genealogy of Genesis 5 and the post-flood genealogy of Genesis 11 (the exception is 2 Chronicles 24:3). That is a real signal and not a coincidence — a chapter that has just crossed a flood and landed is now generating a genealogy in the exact formula Genesis uses on the far side of its own flood — but it cannot be keyed to any single verse, and the formula is the KJV's rather than any one passage's. The observation is adjudicated at 6:18, where it belongs to the Genesis 8-11 sequence argument as a whole. A reader who arrives at 6:15 looking for its source should go there.

'Before they went down to their graves' against 'So they went down to Bethel'. Four words of pure motion-verb-plus-preposition, and the destinations could hardly be further apart: Elisha refusing to leave Elijah on the road to Bethel, and two old men contemplating their burial. Ether 6:19 and 6:21 use the idiom twice in three verses because 'go down to the grave' is the King James way of saying die — “go down to the grave” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 2:6 and Job 21:13, neither of which is in view. Recorded because 2 Kings 2 is a live route in this corpus (1 Nephi 3:15, 1 Nephi 4:2) and a reader might reasonably expect it to be one here.

A tempting one, and worth setting out because two independent things point at it. Genesis 21:11, 'And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son', is the KJV's one sentence in which a father finds a proposal about his son grievous, and Ether 6:23 is 'this was grievous unto them' said of a proposal to make one of their sons a king. “grievous in” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and two of them are this Abraham scene. But the syntax will not carry it: the KJV construction is invariably 'grievous in the sight of' someone, and the Book of Mormon has 'grievous unto them', which is not a KJV idiom at all. And the sense is wrong at the point that matters — Abraham grieves at losing a son, the brother of Jared grieves at one of them being crowned. The 1 Samuel 8:6 parallel, where 'the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, Give us a king', is much the closer situational match and is adjudicated at 6:19; the verse's own borrowing is Revelation 13:10, adjudicated at 6:23.

“a king over them” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and this is the other one: 'And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon.' Listed because the rarity argument at 6:22 depends on the count, and a reader checking it will find this verse and should be told why it was set aside. Judges 9:8 supplies the whole clause the Book of Mormon has — anointing, a king, over them — while Revelation 9:11 supplies only the last four words and supplies them of the locusts of the fifth trumpet. There is a genuine thematic irony in the fact that the KJV's only two kings-over-them are a bramble and Abaddon, and the 6:22 link's significance field makes that point without needing this verse as a source.

The strongest exclusion in the chapter and the one a careful reader would most likely accept. “to be their king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Acts 13:22, 'he raised up unto them David to be their king' — and Ether 6:25 has 'he commanded them that they should constrain no man to be their king'. A four-word singleton in a chapter about making a king is exactly the shape this catalogue normally accepts, and Acts 13 is already a live route in the corpus: Mosiah 29:23 is built out of Acts 13:10, and Acts 13:21, one verse before the singleton, is the New Testament's only retelling of Israel's demand for a king. It is nevertheless declined, for two reasons. The run is a singleton by arithmetic rather than by diction — four of the commonest words in English, in the only order that makes an infinitive of them, and the KJV simply had few occasions to write it. And the sense is not merely different but inverted: Acts 13:22 is God raising a man up to the throne, Ether 6:25 is a father forbidding anyone to be forced onto it. The kingship borrowing in this passage is Judges 9:8, adjudicated at 6:22, and the refusal sequence Judges 9:9-15, adjudicated at 6:26; a reader who arrives at 6:25 should go to both. Noted for a future sweep: if Acts 13:21-22 turns out to stand behind other Jaredite accession formulas, this entry should be revisited.

Ether 6:25 in the 1830 reads 'the first born of the brother of Jared' as two words, which is how Exodus 11:5 spells it in its second occurrence — 'from the first born of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne' — and how 1920 does not, having normalised the Book of Mormon to 'firstborn'. That orthographic agreement is worth recording under CONVENTIONS §8, and it is all there is: 'the firstborn of' is the KJV's standard genitive and Exodus 11:5 is the death of the Egyptian firstborn, which has no bearing on a Jaredite who declines a crown. The Titus 3:2 ('no man to be'), Genesis 37:11 ('him but his father') and 2 Kings 11:17 ('king and the people') candidates at this verse are connective and are passed over under the standing exclusion.

A five-word run whose fifth word is 'to', and the two continuations are 'prosper' and 'commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab'. The Book of Mormon uses 'the people began to' as a narrative hinge throughout — it is one of Mormon's and Moroni's commonest transitions — and Numbers 25:1 is the apostasy at Shittim. No contact. Recorded only because it scored 1.50 and is the top candidate at the verse.

'For all the goodness that the LORD had done for David his servant, and for Israel his people' — and the context is genuinely apt, since 1 Kings 8:66 dismisses the people joyful and glad of heart after a king has dedicated the temple. But the five shared words are the ordinary way of saying what God did for someone, and what identifies Ether 6:30's source is the phrase in front of them, 'how great things', which 1 Kings 8:66 does not have. Adjudicated at 6:30 as 1 Samuel 12:24 in the wording of Mark 5:19; the Mark 5:19 candidate the machine ranked first at this verse is not excluded but is recorded there as the composite and as the live alternative.
